title: WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS
body: The web as a system: what happens between typing a [[URL]] and seeing a page, and how to write code on both ends of that. The course runs the whole stack in order, starting from the wire ([[DNS]], [[HTTP]], [[Stateless Protocol]]), through the document the browser builds from the response ([[HTML]], [[CSS]], the [[DOM]]), into the language that manipulates it ([[JavaScript]]), out to other people's data ([[Fetch]], [[JSON]], [[Web APIs]]), and finally back onto a server of your own ([[Node.js]], [[Express]], [[MongoDB]]). The organising question, and the one worth carrying into every note here: **which machine does this actually happen on?** [[CORS]] is enforced by the browser, not the server. A [[Query String]] is read by the server, a `#fragment` never leaves your laptop. Cookies are attached by the browser without your JavaScript's involvement. Validation on the [[Client]] is a convenience; validation on the [[Server Side]] is the only kind that is real. Almost every confusing thing in web development is that one question in disguise, which is why [[Web Interview Prep]] is built around it too. ## Topics ### The request lifecycle What happens before a single line of your code runs. - [[URL]]: the address, and which machine reads which part of it - [[DNS]]: hostname to [[IP Address]], over UDP, before any HTTP byte is sent - [[IP Address]]: IPv4 exhaustion, private versus public, [[NAT]] - [[HTTP]]: the request/response protocol everything else sits on - [[HTTP Verb]]: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, and which are safe or [[Idempotent]] - [[Stateless Protocol]]: the server remembers nothing, which is the design choice that makes everything else in this course necessary - [[Query String]]: how GET carries parameters, and why credentials never go in one - [[Client]] and [[Server Side]]: the trust boundary, not just a location ### HTML The markup the browser parses into a tree. - [[HTML]]: elements, nesting, structure and semantics only - [[Anchor Tag]]: ``, the thing that makes the web a web - [[Image Tag]]: ``, a second request, and why `width`/`height` prevent layout jump - [[Form Tag]]: `action`, `method`, and GET versus POST for where the values go - [[Input Tag]]: `name` is what gets submitted; client-side validation is not a security control ### CSS and selectors - [[CSS]]: appearance, kept out of the markup - [[CSS Selectors]]: the index of the seven, and the same syntax `querySelector` takes - [[HTML Selector]] · [[Class Selector]] · [[ID Selector]] - [[Descendant Selector]] · [[And Selector]] · [[Attribute Selector]] · [[Pseudo Selector]] ### The DOM The document as live objects in memory, on the user's machine. - [[DOM]]: a [[Tree]] of nodes built from the parsed [[HTML]] - [[Element Node]] and [[Text Node]]: the two node types that matter, and the reason [[firstChild]] surprises people - [[Node Object]]: `id`, `nodeName`, `textContent` - [[NodeList Object]]: array-like, and specifically not an [[Array]] - [[DOM Algorithm]]: select, then modify; every DOM script is that shape - [[Selecting Nodes]]: the legacy `getElementBy*` trio versus `querySelector` / `querySelectorAll` - [[Modifying Documents]]: styles, `classList`, `createElement`, `appendChild`, attributes - [[DOM Performance]]: hoist the query out of the loop - [[Virtual DOM]] and [[Reflow]] are what [[React]] and the browser do about all of this ### Events - [[DOM + Event Handling]]: the second half of every DOM script - [[Event Handling]]: `addEventListener`, and why it beats inline handlers - [[Event Object]]: `e.target`, `preventDefault()`, `stopPropagation()` - [[Event Propagation]]: bubbling up by default, capture going down - [[Event Delegation]]: one handler on the parent instead of a hundred on the children ### JavaScript, the language - [[JavaScript]]: the primitive types, and the fact that everything else is an object - [[JS Functions]]: functions are objects, and [[Hoisting]] is why call-before-declare works - [[Anonymous Function]] · [[Nested Function]] · [[Immediately Invoked Function]] - [[Call Back Function]]: a function passed in to be run later, which is the whole event model - [[Arrow Syntax]]: shorter, and it changes what [[This]] means - [[This]]: four call patterns, four answers, and arrow functions opting out of all of them - [[Closure]]: a function plus the variables captured from where it was **defined** - [[Lexical]]: scope decided by where the code is written, not by who called it - [[Objects]]: the three ways to make one - [[Object Literal]] · [[Object Constructor]] · [[Constructor Functions]] - [[Array Functions]]: `forEach`, `find`, `filter`, `reduce`, `map`, `sort` - [[Shallow copy]]: what `filter` and `map` actually hand back - [[Vanilla JS]]: the language plus the browser, with no framework underneath ### Asynchronous JavaScript - [[Asynchronous JS]]: it happens off the main line of execution, so the value is not there yet - [[Promise]]: pending, fulfilled, rejected, and why `then` chains - [[Fetch]]: consume a web [[API]], get a promise, chain a `.json()` - [[Async Functions]]: `async`/`await` as syntax over the same machinery - [[Parallel Fetches]]: `Promise.all` when two requests do not depend on each other - [[Event Loop]]: why a callback runs later instead of blocking ### APIs and data - [[API]]: the contract, and the boundary between [[Frontend]] and [[Backend]] - [[Web APIs]]: two meanings, third-party HTTP services and the browser's own interfaces - [[JSON]]: text, data only, stricter than JS object syntax - [[CORS]]: the browser refuses cross-origin reads unless the response says otherwise - [[REST]] and [[REST APIs]]: the design conventions the endpoints follow ### Server side - [[Server Side]]: secrets, trust, and shared state can only live here - [[Node.js]]: JavaScript on the server, non-blocking, event driven - [[Node JS]] and [[Server JS]] are the same thing under other names - [[NPM]]: the registry and the CLI that installs everything - [[Module]] and [[Package]]: the unit you require versus the unit npm installs - [[CommonJS]] and [[CommonJS Module]]: `require` / `module.exports`, and the contrast with ES modules - [[Express]]: routes, `req`/`resp`, and not writing raw `writeHead` calls by hand - [[MME]]: the content type that tells the browser what it just received - [[Apache]]: the traditional web server Node replaces in this course - [[PHP]] and [[ASP.NET]]: the older, blocking server environments Node is argued against - [[Cloud]]: where the server actually runs - [[WebSocket Protocol]]: the push architecture HTTP cannot do ### State on a stateless protocol - [[Cookies]]: name/value pairs in HTTP headers, saved by the browser, per domain - [[Cookie Jar]]: the browser's local store, and the reason cookies are untrusted input - [[Session Cookie]]: no expiry, gone when the browser closes - [[Persistent Cookie]]: has an expiry, survives a restart - [[HTTP-Only Cookies]]: page JavaScript cannot read them, which is the [[XSS]] defence - [[Cookies and Browser Storage]] carries the flag-by-flag interview version ### The stack - [[Web Application]]: what all of the above adds up to - [[MERN Stack]]: [[MongoDB]], [[Express]], [[React]], [[Node.js]] - [[MERN]]: the same acronym, spelled without "Stack" - [[MongoDB]]: documents rather than tables, no [[JOIN]] - [[React]]: components, state, and letting a diff decide what to touch ## Core Facts to Know - [[HTTP]] is stateless: every request is self-contained and the server remembers nothing between them. [[Cookies]] exist to fake continuity on top of that. - [[DNS]] resolves the hostname to an [[IP Address]] over UDP **before** any HTTP byte is sent. - The `#fragment` of a [[URL]] is stripped by the browser and never reaches the server. The [[Query String]] is sent and read by the server, and shows up in logs. - GET has no body, so its parameters go in the query string, which is why passwords never go in a GET form. - The [[Client]] is under the user's control. Every check you write in the browser can be deleted by the person you wrote it for. - The [[DOM]] is a [[Tree]] the browser builds from the parsed [[HTML]]; it is not the HTML text itself. - Every DOM script is select, then modify. Wrap it in `DOMContentLoaded` or the nodes are not there yet. - `querySelector` returns one node, `querySelectorAll` returns a [[NodeList Object]]. A NodeList has no `textContent`; you have to iterate it. - A NodeList is array-like but is **not** an [[Array]], so it does not have `map`, `filter`, or `reduce`. - `querySelectorAll` on a selector that matches nothing returns an empty list, not `null`. - [[firstChild]] is usually a whitespace [[Text Node]], not the first element you can see. - Events bubble up to ancestors by default, so one handler on a parent can serve all the children. That is [[Event Delegation]], and it is the fix for a hundred listeners. - `e.target` is the node that generated the event, which is not necessarily the node the listener is attached to. - Function declarations are hoisted, so you can call one above where it is written. `const` and `let` bindings are not usable before their line. - In [[JavaScript]] functions are objects: assignable, passable, and returnable. - A [[Closure]] is a function plus the variables it captured from where it was **defined**, not from where it is called. - [[This]] is decided at call time by how the function was called. Arrow functions have no `this` of their own and take the enclosing one, which is why they cannot be [[Constructor Functions]]. - [[Array Functions]] return new arrays, but the elements inside are the same objects: a [[Shallow copy]]. Mutating an element of the result mutates the original. - `[]` is truthy in JavaScript, so an empty result from `filter` still passes an `if`. - [[Fetch]] returns a [[Promise]] immediately; the response has not arrived on the next line. - `.then` returns a promise, which is the only reason chaining works. - `catch` on a fetch chain does **not** fire on a 404. Check `response.ok` yourself. - `await` must be inside a function marked `async`, and an `async` function always returns a promise, never a bare value. - [[CORS]] is enforced by the **browser**, not by the server. The server merely says `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` and the browser decides whether to hand your JS the response. - [[JSON]] is text and holds data only: no functions, no dates, no `undefined`, and keys must be double-quoted. - [[Node.js]] is non-blocking, which is the whole argument for it over [[PHP]]: one process serves many requests instead of one thread being parked per request. - `require()` returns whatever the required file assigned to `module.exports`. Built-in modules ship with Node; everything else needs [[NPM]] first. - A cookie with an expiry is a [[Persistent Cookie]]; without one it is a [[Session Cookie]] and dies with the browser. - Cookies are attached to matching requests automatically by the browser. Your JavaScript is not involved, which is exactly why [[CSRF]] works. - Anything a cookie contains was in a file on the user's machine, so it arrives as untrusted input. ## Related courses - [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]]: the language fundamentals this course assumes. [[Function]], [[Object]], [[Array]], [[Data type]], [[Encapsulation]], and [[Copying]] all come from there, and [[Shallow copy]] here is the JavaScript instance of a problem C++ hits first. - [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]]: the [[DOM]] is a [[Tree]], and [[Selecting Nodes]] is a traversal. - [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]]: [[Asynchronous JS]] leans on [[Thread]] and on why non-blocking I/O beats one thread per request. Node's event loop is the userspace version of that argument. - [[PROGRAMMING PARADIGMS]]: this is the course that supplies the vault's functional material. [[JS Functions]], [[Closure]], [[Arrow Syntax]], [[Array Functions]], and [[React]] are the worked examples behind that parent's functional section. - [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]]: [[API]] design is a [[Coupling and Cohesion]] question, and the client/server split is the largest interface in the degree. - [[Web Interview Prep]]: the same material re-cut for interviews, organised entirely around which machine each thing runs on. [[HTTP Requests]], [[REST APIs]], [[Cookies and Browser Storage]], [[Modern JavaScript Concepts]], and [[Server-Side Technology]] each extend a section above. --- ## Course material as written Evan's original lecture notes for this file, kept verbatim. The web works through a client-server model. When a user enters a URL, the browser ([[Client]]) sends a request to a Domain Name System [[DNS]] to resolve the website's domain name into an [[IP Address]]. The browser then uses this IP to send an [[HTTP]] request to the web server, which processes the request and sends back a response (often [[HTML]], [[CSS]], [[JavaScript]], etc.). The server-side can include dynamic content generation (e.g., using [[PHP]], [[Node.js]]) and databases for data management. The browser renders the response, showing the user the webpage.
